R_H1.passageTitle: The work of an adult nurse

passages.label: A
passages.text: How does the next nurse know what happened before a shift began? The answer is often in a brief record and a conversation with the care team. An adult nurse may work in a hospital, a health centre or a patient's home, and a doctor and other staff may help the same person. They all need to understand the plan.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Nurses work with people who need different kinds of care, and one nurse may take a patient's temperature or give medicine. On a hard day, a kind voice can help, and a polite question gives someone time to answer. For example, the nurse might ask where it hurts, and the answer can be shared with the next nurse. They can ask each other for advice. Some parts of a day may sound boring until a patient needs a detail to be passed on.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Hospital wards can stay open day and night. Nurses take turns on early, late and weekend shifts, and a nurse needs to stay fit. Healthy habits can help with a busy week. Being good at listening matters too. A person who is afraid may need time to explain what hurts.

passages.label: D
passages.text: A nurse in the United Kingdom usually studies at university. There is work in class and practice with other staff. A high school student can ask a school teacher about useful subjects, or look up courses at school. A nurse must be on the professional register before working. There is more to learn when the work changes.

passages.label: E
passages.text: With time, a nurse may teach new staff or become a ward manager. Some people work in an office. Others stay close to patients. The pay depends on the role. This can be an interesting job for someone who likes doing practical tasks. It can be great to see a patient get well. Pay is part of the job, and what a nurse can earn depends on experience. A young person can talk to a nurse and ask what a day in a ward is like.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A passenger sees a plane at the gate, and an airline pilot has already started work. The captain and crew look at the route, the weather and the amount of fuel on the plane. And they also check what has changed at the airport. These checks let the people working for the company agree on a plan before anyone takes a seat.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Before take-off, a pilot speaks to air traffic control, checks the instruments and follows a written checklist. For example, a warning light can lead the crew to seek advice from an engineer. The job can be hard when the weather changes. A polite message explains the delay to passengers. Clear words help the crew work together. And they also help passengers understand what will happen next.

passages.label: C
passages.text: A pilot works for an airline and may cross several time zones. The job can include nights, weekends and time away from home. Weather or a technical problem may delay a flight. The crew must stay calm. They must make clear what has changed. Long trips can change normal sleep times. The work can be interesting. But the timetable can be hard for a family.

passages.label: D
passages.text: A high school student can start by seeing if they are good at maths and English at school. Training includes flying and work in class. A pilot must be fit and healthy for the work. An aviation doctor checks sight and hearing. A pilot who takes medicine needs to tell the doctor. A language teacher can teach useful habits for clear speech. A kind voice helps a person feel at ease.

passages.label: E
passages.text: An engineer checks the plane. A manager may plan the work in an office. Cabin crew take care of people in the plane. Other staff move the bags. There is a great deal of work to do before a flight. Pay can change with the role and can differ by employer.

R_H3.passageTitle: How a software team builds an app

passages.label: A
passages.text: An app developer may be asked to help a person book a visit to a hospital. When can the patient come? The developer finds out what a nurse and a doctor each need to see, and a manager in the company helps the team agree on a plan. A software engineer then begins to build the app.

passages.label: B
passages.text: A design can start with a few drawings of the screens, and an engineer and an app developer make a first version together. It has to do useful things clearly. The people building it decide where to keep important records and how the screens connect. A person who is good at noticing small details can help at this stage.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Testing starts before the job ends. For example, the team may ask a patient to choose a date for a visit. A kind and polite tester can help the patient explain which words are hard to read. The team can then ask for advice from a nurse and make changes. A journalist reporting on the new app might try the same booking process to see how it works. A second visit can produce more interesting results if changes are tested with a number of users before the app is released. For one person the main problem might just be where to start.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The same process can help people in other jobs. At a school, a school teacher may need large text. A farmer may use an app where there is little internet. A fitness instructor in a gym may need to find a class list quickly. It helps to test the app with those people.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Work goes on after people start to use the app. The team finds and fixes mistakes. People in an office can work with others at home. Some write code. Some talk to users. A person who can explain a fault clearly helps a team work out what to do next.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why does the developer speak to both health workers before the app is built?
options: They have to make the app available for every kind of school.
They can tell the team what information each needs for the job.
They have already found every fault in the finished app.
They must agree to use the same information as every patient.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What choices help turn the drawings into a first version?
options: Which hospital staff will work only on weekends
Which patient will write an article about the app
How to delay each visit until everyone can try the app
Where to keep information and how people will move between screens

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What might a tester learn by letting a patient try the booking process?
options: Where a user finds a step unclear or has trouble reading what to do
How many different versions of the farmer app have already been sold
Whether all future users can avoid reading any of the screens
Why an engineer has to move the records after every appointment

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why could the team try the same procedure again after changing it?
options: Repeating it proves the first version had no faults at all.
After a user points out a problem, everyone else must use that version unchanged.
Trying it again can show how other users get on with the changes before release.
The team can then tell which patient will write the first story about it.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A designer says large text is the only thing that makes an app useful. What does the story suggest instead?
options: Large text eliminates all problems with finding the right step.
What helps depends on the task and setting, so testing should look for other limits as well.
Most apps in the passage are used in identical places for identical tasks.
Using larger letters makes a network connection stronger.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What does the article say about using the fitness instructor example to guide design?
options: Have the instructor try finding a class list and see where the process could be faster.
Make finding class information the last step in every app.
Assume a hospital test gives the exact answer for a gym.
Ask only people with no experience in a gym to choose the task.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What work can still be needed when people have started using the product?
options: Checking what day the first drawing was made
Asking every patient to build a new version alone
Keeping the first release unchanged to avoid more questions
Finding and repairing errors that show up

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What can an explanation from a user add to the teamwork described across the article?
options: It replaces the work of the people creating the software.
It proves that only a person who can write code should describe a problem.
It helps someone identify what went wrong and what part of the app may need attention.
It has a purpose only before the first drawing is made.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A manager says agreeing what to make is enough to know where a patient will get stuck. Which response fits the article?
options: A person trying to book a visit can show a difficulty with reading or starting that an early plan may not show.
Once the staff agree on the information they need, no patient can be confused by the steps.
An engineer can tell where every patient gets stuck without anyone trying the screens.
A person choosing a date can only report what the manager originally planned.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which account makes sense of the team's work from the beginning to after release?
options: The team builds every screen first and then decides what users might need.
The team learns what people need, makes and tests a version, and deals with issues that still appear in use.
Once an app can record a date, no further design or testing is useful.
Writing code and talking with users are given as alternatives that never work together.
